title: Decay or interference? How Peterson and Peterson (1959) read the Brown-Peterson task

blocks.text: In the **Brown-Peterson task**, people study consonants and then count backwards, which blocks rehearsal. The longer the counting, the worse the recall. **Peterson and Peterson (1959)** had to decide why memory got worse.

They judged **interference** an unlikely cause, because counting is so unlike remembering letters. So they concluded that short-term memory loses information through **decay** unless it is rehearsed. This challenged the view, following McGeoch's (1932) critique, that forgetting is due to interference.
The hard part is that the same result can be read two ways. Decay is the researchers' conclusion, not something the task proves, and **Keppel and Underwood (1962)** are cited for an alternative.
children: The result is forgetting with delay. Decay is one reading of it.

title: Sound codes in short-term memory: Conrad (1964), Murray (1968) and Roodenrys et al. (2002)

blocks.text: **Conrad (1964)** and **Murray (1968)** showed the **phonological similarity effect**: lists of similar-sounding letters are recalled worse than lists of different-sounding ones, even when read silently. So people **recode what they see into a speech-based form**. If the code were visual, the mix-ups would be between look-alikes such as E and F instead.

The effect disappears when people use **articulatory suppression** on visually presented lists, because that occupies the articulatory control process that converts visual input to speech. This is the basis of the **phonological loop**, with its phonological store and articulatory control process.

**Roodenrys et al. (2002)** add a twist. Words from **large neighborhoods**, like cat, are recalled better than words from small neighborhoods, like hippopotamus. A neighbor differs by one letter or one sound, so long-term knowledge of words helps short-term recall.
children: Memory span is not a pure measure of short-term capacity.

title: Substitution or error sensitivity? Hoover and Healy (2019)

blocks.text: In the **bat-and-ball problem** (Frederick, 2005), a bat and ball cost $1.10 and the bat costs $1.00 more. The intuitive answer is 10 cents, but the correct answer is 5 cents. Kahneman and Frederick (2002) called the error **unconscious attribute substitution**, and De Neys and colleagues (2013) found wrong reasoners were less confident than on a control version.

**Hoover and Healy (2019)** tested whether people simply overlook 'more than'. Wrong reasoners **mostly remembered 'more than'**, so it was not unconsciously ignored. Because substitution cannot be confirmed as the cause of the error, they prefer the term **error sensitivity**.
children: The error is real, but the substitution explanation is not confirmed.

title: Peers and the adolescent brain: Chein et al. (2011) and Albert, Chein and Steinberg (2013)

blocks.text: Adolescents take more risks when friends are around. The question is whether peers weaken reasoning or change something else.

**Chein and colleagues (2011)** scanned people playing a driving game alone or watched by friends. Adolescents took more risks when watched, with **greater reward-region activity**. **Cognitive-control regions did not change** with peers, so the authors concluded the effect works mainly through **reward circuitry**.
**Albert, Chein and Steinberg (2013)** argue the same point from behavior: adolescents reason about risk like adults in the lab, and the **peer context** is what raises risk taking.
children: The peer context changes the reward response, not the reasoning.

title: Framing and defaults together: Giuliani et al. (2023)

blocks.text: The **framing effect** means gain wording pushes people to the sure option and loss wording to the gamble. The **default effect** means people tend to choose the preselected option. **Giuliani and colleagues (2023)** combined them to see how they work together.
A **risky default raised risk taking**, a sure default did not raise risk aversion, and the two effects were **additive**. So the effects add up rather than one cancelling the other.

An exploratory question, asked after the choice, found that belief about the default's origin went with following or rejecting it. The hard part is that this question came after the choice, so it may be a justification rather than a cause.
**Cognitive offloading** means using actions like writing things down to reduce mental demands (Risko and Gilbert, 2016). **Morrison and Richmond (2020)** asked who offloads and whether it helps.

**Offloading improved memory**, especially at high loads, and people offloaded more as load grew. The surprise is that **memory ability did not predict who offloaded**. Low-capacity people were expected to offload more, but they did not.
children: So offloading may be a compensatory strategy across abilities.
